JP.summary: Japan made using cannabis a crime on December 12, 2024, when it reclassified cannabis and THC as narcotics. Possession, use and transfer each carry up to 7 years in prison. The same reform allows approved cannabis-derived medicines.
JP.note: Japanese sources are summarized in English.

adult-use.short: No. Using it is a crime since December 2024
adult-use.detail: The revised laws that took effect on December 12, 2024 classify cannabis and THC as narcotics and add a crime of use, which did not exist before. Use, possession and transfer each carry up to 7 years in prison, up from 5 years for possession.
adult-use.citation: Revised Cannabis Control Act and Narcotics and Psychotropics Control Act (2024); MHLW; Nippon.com/Jiji

medical.short: Only approved cannabis-derived medicines
medical.detail: The reform lifted the ban on cannabis-derived medicines once their efficacy and safety are confirmed; before it, such medicines were allowed only in clinical trials. CBD is not treated as a narcotic, but smokable plant material and resin are.
medical.citation: Revised laws (2024); Nippon.com/Jiji; DIA Global Forum (Feb 2025)

possession.short: Any amount: up to 7 years
possession.detail: Possession of any amount is a crime punishable by up to 7 years in prison; import carries 1 to 10 years. The UK government warns of zero tolerance, that police may charge people whose blood shows an illegal substance, and that small quantities received by post have led to arrests.
possession.citation: MHLW notice to foreign residents; UK FCDO travel advice

home-grow.short: Only licensed growers
home-grow.detail: Growing cannabis needs a licence. The 2024 reform split cultivation licences into two kinds during 2025: for raw materials for cannabis-plant products and for medicines.
home-grow.citation: Jiji Press (Dec 12 2024)

IN.name: India
IN.summary: India bans cannabis flowers (ganja) and resin (charas) under the 1985 NDPS Act, with penalties scaled by quantity. The leaves and seeds are outside the federal definition, so bhang is left to the states: some license bhang shops, others ban it.
IN.note: Several sources here are legal explainers rather than the statute itself; they agree on the structure of the law.

adult-use.short: No, except bhang where a state allows it
adult-use.detail: Producing, possessing, selling, buying, transporting and using ganja and charas are offences under the NDPS Act. Leaves and seeds are excluded from its definition of cannabis, and states regulate them: Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan have authorised bhang shops, while Assam's own law bans both ganja and bhang.
adult-use.citation: NDPS Act 1985, s. 2 and s. 20 (Nyaaya; The News Minute; SCC Online)

medical.short: Ayurvedic preparations under licence
medical.detail: The Ministry of AYUSH permits cannabis in medicinal preparations, subject to the legal framework and state rules. This guide has not yet checked how patients obtain them.
medical.citation: GKToday summary of NDPS Act and AYUSH rules

possession.short: Up to 1 kg of ganja is a "small quantity"
possession.detail: Penalties depend on the amount. A small quantity, up to 1 kg of ganja or 100 g of charas, carries up to 1 year in prison, a fine of up to Rs 10,000, or both. Above that but below commercial quantity (20 kg of ganja, 1 kg of charas) carries up to 10 years and a fine of up to Rs 1 lakh. The UK government warns British travellers of a minimum of 6 months for small personal amounts.
possession.citation: NDPS Act, s. 20 (Nyaaya; The News Minute); UK FCDO travel advice

home-grow.short: Growing the plant is a crime
home-grow.detail: Cultivating the cannabis plant is an offence even though bhang made from its leaves can be legal. In 2025 the Kerala High Court dismissed a petition from a man caught with five plants on his terrace.
home-grow.citation: NDPS Act (Vajiram & Ravi summary, Nov 2025)

NP.name: Nepal
NP.summary: Cannabis has been illegal in Nepal since the Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act of 1976, and even small amounts can mean years in prison. In 2026 Gandaki province passed its own law to license medical and industrial cultivation, and the Supreme Court ordered the federal government to write cultivation rules.
NP.note: Nepali sources are summarized in English. The national ban and the provincial law were still in tension when this was checked.

adult-use.short: No
adult-use.detail: The 1976 Act prohibits growing, producing, buying, selling, storing and using cannabis.
adult-use.citation: Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act 1976 (Substance Abuse and Rehabilitation, 2024)

medical.short: A provincial law and a court order, not yet a national program
medical.detail: In 2026 Gandaki province legalised licensed farming and use of cannabis for medical purposes despite the national ban, with five-year licences for registered companies. The 1976 Act allows special licences only to the national government or institutions under its full supervision. On November 2, 2026 the Supreme Court ordered the government to write cultivation rules under the Act within three months.
medical.citation: AP (Aug 5 2026); My Republica; Kathmandu Post (Aug 12 2026); Supreme Court order (Nov 2 2026)

possession.short: Even small amounts: prison possible
possession.detail: Possession is a crime under the 1976 Act. The UK government warns that being caught with even small amounts of marijuana can mean more than 5 years in prison, and that police may seize and charge over products containing CBD.
possession.citation: UK FCDO travel advice; Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act 1976

home-grow.short: No. Unlicensed growing is a federal crime
home-grow.detail: Growing is prohibited under the 1976 Act. Even under Gandaki's law, cultivating without a licence is punished under the federal Act.
home-grow.citation: Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act 1976; My Republica (2026)

SG.name: Singapore
SG.summary: Singapore has zero tolerance for cannabis. Consumption alone carries up to 10 years in prison, drug use detected on arrival can mean arrest, and trafficking can bring the death penalty. Only approved cannabinoid medicines, case by case, are allowed.

adult-use.short: No. Zero tolerance
adult-use.detail: The government has strict laws against trafficking, possession, consumption, import and export of cannabis and cannabis products. Cannabis is a Class A drug: consumption carries up to 10 years in prison and a fine of up to S$20,000.
adult-use.citation: Misuse of Drugs Act (CNB; MHA)

medical.short: Only approved cannabinoid medicines, case by case
medical.detail: The government separates raw cannabis, which it says is not medically validated, from pharmaceutical cannabinoid products, which may be used only under strict assessment and approval. In 2019 a girl with drug-resistant epilepsy became the first patient approved, after her doctor applied to the Health Sciences Authority.
medical.citation: MHA position; CNB; Mothership (Dec 2019)

possession.short: Any amount, including drugs in your system
possession.detail: The UK government warns that people carrying drugs can be imprisoned, caned or executed, and that drug use detected on arrival or in transit leads to refusal of entry or arrest. The US State Department gives similar warnings.
possession.citation: UK FCDO travel advice; US State Department advisory

MY.name: Malaysia
MY.summary: Malaysia has some of the world's strictest drug laws, with long prison terms, caning and the death penalty. Since 2021 the Health Ministry has said registered cannabis-based medicines can be prescribed, but none is known to be widely available.

adult-use.short: No
adult-use.detail: The Dangerous Drugs Act, Poisons Act and Sale of Drugs Act prohibit possessing, planting, harvesting and processing cannabis.
adult-use.citation: Medical Journal of Malaysia (2026), summarising the three Acts

medical.short: Legal only for registered products on prescription
medical.detail: The Health Ministry says the law does not bar medical use: a product must be registered with the Drug Control Authority, imported under licence, and sold only on prescription by a registered doctor or a pharmacist with a Type A licence. In March 2025 it invited registration applications backed by enough scientific evidence. A 2026 medical-journal article says import of cannabis-based medicines is otherwise allowed only for research or clinical trials.
medical.citation: Health Ministry statements (CodeBlue, Nov 2021; The Star, Mar 2025); Medical Journal of Malaysia (2026)

possession.short: Any amount, even in transit
possession.detail: Possessing, using, trafficking, importing or exporting cannabis is illegal, including while transiting. The UK government lists penalties of up to 20 years in prison, caning and the death penalty; Australia also lists Malaysia among countries with the death penalty for drug offences.
possession.citation: UK FCDO travel advice; Australian Smartraveller

home-grow.short: No
home-grow.detail: Planting and harvesting cannabis are prohibited under the Dangerous Drugs Act.
home-grow.citation: Medical Journal of Malaysia (2026)

PH.name: Philippines
PH.summary: Cannabis is illegal in the Philippines under the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act (RA 9165), and even a small amount means a mandatory prison sentence. The only medical route is a special permit from the Food and Drug Administration; bills to create a medical program were advancing in 2026.

adult-use.short: No
adult-use.detail: Possession, use, cultivation and distribution of cannabis are illegal under RA 9165.
adult-use.citation: RA 9165 (Respicio & Co., Jan 2026)

medical.short: Only with an FDA compassionate special permit
medical.detail: The Department of Health allows medical use only under a compassionate special permit signed by the FDA director general, which needs a doctor's prescription and records of the patient's condition. House committees approved a medical cannabis bill in February 2026; it was not law when checked.
medical.citation: FDA compassionate special permit (Philstar, Feb 2024; Respicio & Co., Jan 2026); Manila Times (Feb 25 2026)

possession.short: Even a small amount: mandatory prison
possession.detail: The UK government warns that a conviction for possessing even a small amount of any illicit drug means a mandatory prison sentence.
possession.citation: UK FCDO travel advice

home-grow.short: No
home-grow.detail: Cultivation is illegal under RA 9165.
home-grow.citation: RA 9165 (Respicio & Co., Jan 2026)

AE.name: United Arab Emirates
AE.summary: The UAE has zero tolerance for drugs. Possessing even the smallest amount of cannabis can mean at least 3 months in prison or a heavy fine, traces in your blood count as possession, and some CBD products are illegal.

adult-use.short: No. Zero tolerance
adult-use.detail: The UK government says there is zero tolerance for drug offences, with severe penalties for using, possessing, smuggling and trafficking, including the death penalty for trafficking.
adult-use.citation: UK FCDO travel advice

possession.short: Any amount, including traces in your blood
possession.detail: Possession of even the smallest amount, including cannabis, can lead to a minimum 3-month prison term or a fine of 20,000 to 100,000 dirhams. The authorities count drugs found in your bloodstream as possession, so use before arrival can lead to charges.
possession.citation: UK FCDO travel advice (updated Nov 18 2026)

ID.name: Indonesia
ID.summary: Indonesia has zero tolerance for drugs. Possessing, using, making or trafficking cannabis can bring long prison sentences or the death penalty, and airports scan transit passengers' bags.

adult-use.short: No. Zero tolerance
adult-use.detail: The UK government warns not to get involved with illegal drugs in Indonesia: possession, use, manufacture and trafficking can bring long prison sentences or the death penalty.
adult-use.citation: UK FCDO travel advice

possession.short: Any amount: long prison or death
possession.detail: Possession of any amount is an offence; penalties include long prison sentences and, for serious cases, the death penalty. Airports scan the bags of transit passengers.
possession.citation: UK FCDO travel advice

SA.name: Saudi Arabia
SA.summary: Saudi Arabia has zero tolerance for drugs. Possessing even a small amount can mean up to 5 years in prison and a large fine, and dealing or smuggling can bring a death sentence.

adult-use.short: No. Zero tolerance
adult-use.detail: The UK government says there is zero tolerance for drug offences and the penalties are severe, with long detention possible before trial.
adult-use.citation: UK FCDO travel advice

possession.short: Up to 5 years, even for small amounts
possession.detail: Possessing even small amounts can bring up to 5 years in prison and a fine of 30,000 riyals. Drug dealing and smuggling can result in a death sentence.
possession.citation: UK FCDO travel advice (updated Nov 18 2026)

CN.name: China
CN.summary: China has zero tolerance for drugs, including cannabis. People caught face heavy fines, long prison sentences or the death penalty, and airports scan for cannabis.

adult-use.short: No. Zero tolerance
adult-use.detail: Possession, trafficking and manufacture of any illegal drug, including cannabis, are serious offences under a zero-tolerance policy.
adult-use.citation: UK FCDO travel advice

possession.short: Any amount: fines, prison or death
possession.detail: Those caught face heavy fines, lengthy prison sentences or the death penalty. Australia also lists China among countries that apply the death penalty to drug offences.
possession.citation: UK FCDO travel advice; Australian Smartraveller

TR.name: Türkiye
TR.summary: Cannabis is illegal in Türkiye. The UK government warns of 4 to 24 years in prison and heavy fines for possessing, using or smuggling drugs, including when transiting through airports.

adult-use.short: No
adult-use.detail: Illegal drugs, including cannabis, carry severe penalties for possession, use and smuggling.
adult-use.citation: UK FCDO travel advice

possession.short: 4 to 24 years possible
possession.detail: The UK government says to expect a long prison sentence of 4 to 24 years and heavy fines for possessing, using or smuggling illegal drugs, including in transit; airports scan transit baggage.
possession.citation: UK FCDO travel advice (updated Nov 18 2026)

PL.name: Poland
PL.summary: Possession of any amount of cannabis is a crime in Poland, though prosecutors may drop small personal-use cases. Medical cannabis has been available on prescription from pharmacies since 2017.

adult-use.short: No
adult-use.detail: Recreational use is not allowed and is subject to criminal liability under the Act on Counteracting Drug Addiction of 2005.
adult-use.citation: Act on Counteracting Drug Addiction 2005 (EUDA 2017; CMS)

medical.short: On prescription, prepared by pharmacies
medical.detail: Medical cannabis is dispensed by pharmacies as a prescription medicine, prepared in the pharmacy from a doctor's prescription.
medical.citation: CMS Expert Guide: Poland

possession.short: Up to 3 years; small cases may be dropped
possession.detail: Any drug possession, even a small amount for personal use, carries up to 3 years in prison; a minor offence can bring a fine, restriction of liberty or up to 1 year; a substantial amount up to 12 years. Prosecutors may discontinue cases involving small amounts for personal use, but do not have to.
possession.citation: Act on Counteracting Drug Addiction (EUDA Country Drug Report 2017)

GR.name: Greece
GR.summary: Recreational cannabis is illegal in Greece, but the 2013 drug law treats personal use more leniently than dealing. Licensed medical cannabis production has been legal since 2018, and prescription cannabis became available in pharmacies in 2024.

adult-use.short: No
adult-use.detail: Possession, use and smuggling are offences; the UK government warns of jail and heavy fines, including when transiting airports.
adult-use.citation: Law 4139/2013; UK FCDO travel advice

medical.short: Prescription cannabis from pharmacies since 2024
medical.detail: Law 4523/2018 allowed licensed production of medicinal cannabis end-products. Prescription cannabis became available in pharmacies in early 2024, about two years after the plan was announced.
medical.citation: Law 4523/2018; Greek Reporter (Feb 25 2024)

possession.short: Personal use punished more leniently; a judge decides the amount
possession.detail: Law 4139/2013 separates possession for personal use from possession for sale and sets milder sanctions for personal use. It dropped fixed personal-use quantities; judges decide based on the substance, its quantity and purity, and the person's needs.
possession.citation: Law 4139/2013 (EUDA Country Drug Report 2018)

NO.name: Norway
NO.summary: Cannabis is illegal in Norway, but small personal amounts usually bring a fine. Two cannabis medicines are approved, and doctors can apply for special permits for others.

adult-use.short: No
adult-use.detail: Recreational use is not allowed. A 2021 government proposal to decriminalise possession of small amounts for personal use did not become law.
adult-use.citation: CMS Expert Guide: Norway

medical.short: Two approved medicines; others by special permit
medical.detail: Doctors who can prescribe group A medicines can prescribe the approved cannabis medicines Sativex and Epidyolex, and can apply for a special permit for named patients to use other cannabis products. Other uses are treated as experimental.
medical.citation: Norwegian Medical Products Agency

possession.short: Up to 15 g usually means a fine
possession.detail: Possession and use carry up to 6 months in prison, but possessing a small amount, up to 15 grams, for personal use is usually punished only with a fine, especially for first offences.
possession.citation: Penal Code and Medicines Act (CMS)

SE.name: Sweden
SE.summary: Sweden prohibits cannabis even in small amounts and enforces minor drug offences more than its Nordic neighbours. A few cannabis medicines are available on prescription or under licence.

adult-use.short: No
adult-use.detail: Illegal drugs, including cannabis, are strictly prohibited even in small quantities; use itself is an offence.
adult-use.citation: UK FCDO travel advice; Nordic Welfare Centre (2019)

medical.short: A few medicines on prescription or licence
medical.detail: Sativex is used for multiple sclerosis spasms, and Marinol can be prescribed under licence.
medical.citation: Nordic Welfare Centre (2019)

possession.short: Minor offence: fine or up to 6 months
possession.detail: Penalties depend on the amount and how dangerous the substance is judged to be; a minor drug offence carries a fine or up to 6 months in prison. The UK government warns of sentences of up to 10 years for serious cases.
possession.citation: Narcotic Drugs Punishments Act (Nordic Welfare Centre); UK FCDO travel advice

FI.name: Finland
FI.summary: Using, possessing and growing cannabis are crimes in Finland under the Criminal Code. Medical cannabis is available only as Sativex or through individual special permits from the medicines agency.

adult-use.short: No
adult-use.detail: Drug use has been a crime since 1966; the Criminal Code covers use, possession, manufacturing, growing, smuggling and selling.
adult-use.citation: Criminal Code (Nordic Welfare Centre)

medical.short: Sativex, or a special permit from Fimea
medical.detail: Sativex has a marketing authorisation. Other medical cannabis is an unlicensed medicine that needs a special permit from the Finnish Medicines Agency, granted patient by patient.
medical.citation: Prohibition Partners (Oct 2025)

possession.short: Prohibited even in small amounts
possession.detail: Possession and use are offences even in small quantities. The UK government warns of sentences of up to 10 years and heavy fines for serious cases.
possession.citation: Criminal Code (Nordic Welfare Centre); UK FCDO travel advice

home-grow.short: No
home-grow.detail: Growing cannabis is an offence under the Criminal Code.
home-grow.citation: Criminal Code (Nordic Welfare Centre)

GU.name: Guam
GU.summary: Guam, a U.S. territory, legalised medical cannabis in 2014 and adult use in 2019. Adults 21 and over may possess up to an ounce and grow at home, but the licensed market has been slow to open. Federal law still applies, including at the airport.
GU.note: U.S. federal law still prohibits cannabis, and federal agents work at airports and ports in the territories.

adult-use.short: Yes, 21 and over
adult-use.detail: The Guam Cannabis Industries Act, signed on April 4, 2019, legalised personal possession by adults and set rules for licensed production and retail sale.
adult-use.citation: Guam Cannabis Industries Act 2019 (NORML; MPP)

medical.short: Yes, since 2014
medical.detail: Guam was the first U.S. territory to legalise medical cannabis, in 2014. Patients may possess 2.5 ounces and grow up to six mature and 12 immature plants. NORML lists licensed dispensaries as allowed but not yet operating.
medical.citation: NORML; MPP

possession.short: Up to 1 ounce
possession.detail: Adults may possess up to one ounce, plus what their own plants produce. Having more than an ounce is a petty misdemeanour with up to 60 days in jail and a fine of up to $500.
possession.citation: Guam Pub. L. 35-05 (NORML)

home-grow.short: Six plants, three flowering
home-grow.detail: Adults may grow six plants at a time, three flowering and three immature, in private.
home-grow.citation: Weedmaps summary (secondary)

MP.name: Northern Mariana Islands
MP.summary: The Northern Mariana Islands, a U.S. commonwealth, legalised cannabis for medical and adult use in September 2018, the first U.S. territory to legalise adult use by legislation. Federal law still applies.
MP.note: U.S. federal law still prohibits cannabis.

adult-use.short: Yes, 21 and over
adult-use.detail: The governor signed the Taulamwaar Sensible CNMI Cannabis Act into law on September 21, 2018, legalising cannabis for medical purposes and adult use. Business licences require 10 years of continued residency, with exceptions for military service and education.
adult-use.citation: Taulamwaar Sensible CNMI Cannabis Act 2018 (MPP)

medical.short: Yes
medical.detail: The same 2018 law covers medical use.
medical.citation: MPP

home-grow.short: Yes, registered home growers
home-grow.detail: Adults may grow at home after registering with the Cannabis Commission; plants may not be in public view and must be secured from anyone under 21.
home-grow.citation: Taulamwaar Sensible CNMI Cannabis Act 2018 (MPP summary)

VI.name: U.S. Virgin Islands
VI.summary: The U.S. Virgin Islands legalised adult-use cannabis on January 18, 2023, alongside medical and sacramental use, under one regulator. Possession is legal for adults 21 and over; the first licensed dispensaries were expected to open by the end of 2026. Federal law still applies.
VI.note: U.S. federal law still prohibits cannabis.

adult-use.short: Yes, 21 and over (residents and visitors)
adult-use.detail: The Virgin Islands Cannabis Use Act (Act 8680), signed on January 18, 2023, allows cannabis for medicinal, sacramental and adult use and regulates production and sale through the Office of Cannabis Regulation.
adult-use.citation: Act 8680 (Government House; Office of Cannabis Regulation)

medical.short: Yes, with higher limits
medical.detail: Medical cannabis was legalised in 2019 and folded into the 2023 Act. Qualified patients may possess more than other adults: 4 ounces of flower, 1 ounce of concentrate and 2 ounces of cannabis products.
medical.citation: Act 8680 (VibeHigh summary, secondary)

possession.short: 2 oz flower, 14 g concentrate
possession.detail: Adults 21 and over may possess up to 2 ounces of flower, 14 grams of concentrate and 1 ounce of cannabis products, with no card required.
possession.citation: Act 8680 (VibeHigh summary, secondary)

buying.short: Stores were expected to open by the end of 2026
buying.detail: In August 2026 the Office of Cannabis Regulation told legislators that licensed cultivation could begin within weeks and at least two dispensaries might open before the end of 2026, but sales cannot start until a testing laboratory is operating.
buying.citation: VI Consortium (Aug 2026)

PR.name: Puerto Rico
PR.summary: Puerto Rico, a U.S. territory, has had a medical cannabis program since 2015, run by its Department of Health. This guide has not yet reviewed the rules for adult use or possession there. Federal law still applies.
PR.note: U.S. federal law still prohibits cannabis.

medical.short: Yes, since 2015
medical.detail: The governor signed a medical cannabis measure in 2015 and the Department of Health implemented it. There were 114,274 registered patients in March 2021.
medical.citation: MPP

AG.name: Antigua and Barbuda
AG.summary: Since March 2018, having up to 15 grams of cannabis is not an offence, a household may grow up to four plants, and old convictions for 15 grams or less were expunged. Smoking in public is still an offence and there is no legal recreational sale. A licensed medical system and registered religious use, mainly by Rastafari, run under the Cannabis Act.
AG.note: The two Acts are cited from gazetted copies hosted outside the government's own site.

adult-use.short: Decriminalised in private; no recreational sale
adult-use.detail: The Misuse of Drugs (Amendment) Act 2018 made possession of up to 15 grams of cannabis or resin no offence. Smoking cannabis in a public place, including bars, restaurants, clubs, tourist establishments and government buildings, is still an offence: a police warning first, then a $500 ticket, then a fine of up to $1,500, and these do not go on a criminal record. The Cannabis Act 2018 bans recreational use outside its medical and religious schemes, and there is no legal recreational sale. A child under 18 found with cannabis must attend a drug counselling programme.
adult-use.citation: Misuse of Drugs (Amendment) Act 2018, ss. 6A-6C; Cannabis Act 2018, s. 60

medical.short: Licensed dispensaries for registered patients
medical.detail: The Cannabis Act 2018 set up the Medicinal Cannabis Authority to license cultivation, dispensaries, lounges, processing, testing, transport and import or export. A patient with a qualifying condition gets a recommendation from a doctor registered with the Authority, then an identification card valid for up to a year. Visitors with a valid recommendation from another country can get a visitor card and use an authorised dispensary. The first production licence went to Grow Antigua on June 14, 2021.
medical.citation: Cannabis Act 2018, ss. 13-14, 45-48, 56-57; Antigua Newsroom (licence of Jun 14 2021)

buying.detail: There is no legal recreational sale. Medicinal cannabis is sold through licensed dispensaries to card holders, with a 15% sales tax. Unlicensed cultivation for supply, dispensing or transport carries a fine of up to $75,000 or up to 2 years in prison.
buying.citation: Cannabis Act 2018, ss. 44, 56, 60

possession.short: Up to 15 grams is not an offence
possession.detail: A person with no more than 15 grams of cannabis or cannabis resin is not guilty of an offence and no penalty applies, subject to the public smoking rules. Registered religious adherents may hold more with authorisation from the Medicinal Cannabis Authority.
possession.citation: Misuse of Drugs (Amendment) Act 2018, s. 6A; Cannabis Act 2018, ss. 3, 7

home-grow.short: Up to four plants per household
home-grow.detail: The head of a household, owner, tenant or other person in control of the property where they live may grow up to four cannabis plants per household on that property. Registered religious bodies can be authorised to grow more for sacramental use, without any commercial activity.
home-grow.citation: Misuse of Drugs (Amendment) Act 2018, s. 5 (new s. 8(1A)); Cannabis Act 2018, ss. 3-5

driving.short: No driving under the influence
driving.detail: The Cannabis Act prohibits operating any motor vehicle, aircraft or boat under the influence of cannabis, and using cannabis in any motor vehicle. Breaches carry a fine of up to $75,000 or up to 2 years.
driving.citation: Cannabis Act 2018, s. 60(1)(c), (e) and (4)

record-relief.short: Old convictions for 15 grams or less were expunged
record-relief.detail: The 2018 amendment treats convictions from before the Act for 15 grams or less of cannabis or resin as spent and expunged, despite the general rehabilitation-of-offenders law.
record-relief.citation: Misuse of Drugs (Amendment) Act 2018, s. 7 (new s. 39)

border.short: Do not carry cannabis in or out
border.detail: Importing or exporting cannabis needs written authorisation from the Minister or an import/export licence. Visitors who buy medicinal cannabis on a visitor card may not take it out of the country.

experiment.text: Rastafari groups were granted licences in 2023 to grow cannabis for religious use, and registered adherents can use it at places of worship, private homes and declared religious events.

differences.title: What is different about Antigua and Barbuda
points: Home growing of up to four plants is lawful, not just tolerated.
Old small-possession convictions were wiped automatically.
Religious use has its own legal track, with sacramental dispensaries that may not make a profit.
Visitors with a recommendation from home can buy from a medical dispensary but cannot take it with them.

KN.name: Saint Kitts and Nevis
KN.summary: Small amounts and up to five plants carry no criminal sanction. Adults can also take out a licence under the Freedom of Conscience (Cannabis) Act 2023 to carry up to 56 grams in permitted public places, smoke in designated smoking areas and grow up to five plants at home; fees are waived until the end of 2026. Rastafari sacramental use is recognised in law, and a Medicinal Cannabis Authority licenses sales.
KN.note: Two of the laws are cited from the bill texts the government published; the final enacted wording was not opened.

adult-use.short: Decriminalised, with an optional adult licence
adult-use.detail: The government says individuals may possess small quantities and grow up to five plants without criminal sanctions. Adults aged 18 or over can also apply to the Ministry responsible for faith-based affairs for a two-year licence under the Freedom of Conscience (Cannabis) Act 2023. A seven-day temporary licence also exists. Licence fees are waived until December 31, 2026. Unauthorised sales remain illegal.
adult-use.citation: SKNIS (Apr 28 2025); Freedom of Conscience (Cannabis) Bill 2023, ss. 2-5; Government notice (Apr 2 2026)

medical.short: A Medicinal Cannabis Authority licenses the industry
medical.detail: The Medicinal Cannabis Authority was launched on April 25, 2025, under the Ministry of Agriculture, to license a regulated medicinal cannabis industry for patients with authorised prescriptions. Legal sales are permitted only through licensed entities.
medical.citation: SKNIS (Apr 28 2025)

buying.detail: Legal cannabis sales are permitted only through entities licensed under the Cannabis Act, and the government has named cannabis lounges as a new opportunity. Unauthorised sales remain illegal and are enforced by the police.
buying.citation: SKNIS (Apr 28 2025)

possession.short: Small amounts are not a crime; licence holders up to 56 grams
possession.detail: The 2019 amendment to the Drugs Act, passed on July 31, 2019, replaced prosecution for up to 15 grams of cannabis or 5 grams of resin with a $50 fixed penalty notice in the bill as published. The government described small-quantity possession in 2025 as carrying no criminal sanction. A Freedom of Conscience licence lets an adult carry up to 56 grams of cannabis or 15 grams of resin in permitted public places, which exclude schools, hospitals, churches, police and government offices and similar places.
possession.citation: Drugs (Amendment) Bill 2019, s. 6A(2); SKNIS (Aug 1 2019; Apr 28 2025); Freedom of Conscience (Cannabis) Bill 2023, ss. 2-3

home-grow.short: Up to five plants
home-grow.detail: The government says up to five plants can be grown without criminal sanction. With a Freedom of Conscience licence, an adult may grow five or fewer plants in a secured area of their private premises, kept away from minors and vulnerable people. Going over the limit, or failing to secure the plants, falls back under the Drugs Act.
home-grow.citation: SKNIS (Apr 28 2025); Freedom of Conscience (Cannabis) Bill 2023, ss. 3, 7

driving.short: Impaired driving falls under traffic law
driving.detail: The 2019 Drugs Act amendment, as published, leaves impaired driving to the Vehicles and Road Traffic Act, and sets heavy fines for using cannabis in schools, on school buses and near schools during school hours.
driving.citation: Drugs (Amendment) Bill 2019, s. 6B

experiment.text: Smoking in public is the line to watch: outside designated smoking areas it drew a $1,000 fixed penalty in the 2019 bill, and three tickets for it can cost a Freedom of Conscience licence.

differences.title: What is different about Saint Kitts and Nevis
points: Adult use is framed as freedom of conscience, with a licence issued by the ministry for faith-based affairs.
Rastafari sacramental use is recognised in its own 2023 Act, with free permits.
A short temporary licence exists alongside the two-year licence.

VC.name: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
VC.summary: Possession of up to 56 grams (two ounces) is still illegal but only a ticketable offence: no arrest and no criminal record. Smoking at home and at Rastafari places of worship is not punished, but smoking in public is unlawful. A Medicinal Cannabis Authority set up in 2019 licenses a medical industry, including dispensaries and a consumption lounge for card holders. The government rejects full legalisation.
VC.note: The amended Drugs (Prevention of Misuse) Act was not opened; possession rules come from news reports and police statements.

adult-use.short: Decriminalised at home; not legal
adult-use.detail: Since a 2019 amendment to the Drugs (Prevention of Misuse) Act, smoking cannabis in private homes and at Rastafari places of worship is not punished. Section 7C makes it unlawful to smoke or use cannabis in any public place, though the Minister may designate public areas, and police may ask people to move somewhere private. Prime Minister Gonsalves said in April 2025 that the government permits small quantities for personal use but will not legalise.
adult-use.citation: Drugs (Prevention of Misuse) Act as amended in 2019, reported by Searchlight (Aug 2 2019; Dec 13 2024); gov.vc (Apr 17 2025)

medical.short: Prescription plus an Authority ID card
medical.detail: Parliament passed a medicinal cannabis industry law on December 11, 2018, and the Medicinal Cannabis Authority was established in 2019 to regulate cultivation, manufacture and compliance. A patient with a prescription applies to the Authority for a cannabis ID card valid for one year, then buys from a licensed dispensary. In 2022 the first consumption lounge opened, with on-site doctor consultations.
medical.citation: Searchlight (Aug 2 2019); gov.vc (Apr 17 2025); Jamaica Observer (May 7 2022)

buying.detail: There is no recreational market. Medicinal cannabis is sold by licensed dispensaries to people with a Medicinal Cannabis Authority ID card, and people with a medical prescription may smoke in designated areas.
buying.citation: Jamaica Observer (May 7 2022); Searchlight (Dec 13 2024)

possession.short: Up to 56 grams is a ticket, not an arrest
possession.detail: Possession of 56 grams or less remains illegal but is ticketable: no arrest, no detention and no criminal record. A person who admits it gets a health and education card and has a month to pay an $80 ticket; under-18s and people who seem dependent are pointed to counselling. A person who denies it is summoned to court, where the maximum fine is $500. Any amount on school, medical, sporting or cultural premises with students present is still treated as trafficking unless proven otherwise.
possession.citation: Searchlight (Aug 2 2019; Dec 13 2024)

experiment.text: Alongside the medical law, Parliament passed a separate amnesty Act in December 2018 for traditional cannabis growers.

differences.title: What is different about Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
points: Up to 56 grams is handled with a ticket and leaves no criminal record.
Traditional growers were offered an amnesty when the medical law passed.
The government frames its reforms as staying inside the UN drug conventions.

TT.name: Trinidad and Tobago
TT.summary: Under a 2019 law, having up to 30 grams of cannabis or 5 grams of resin, and growing up to four plants, is not an offence. Larger amounts and smoking in public carry fines, often settled with a fixed penalty ticket, and old small-possession records were ordered expunged. A Cannabis Control Act for medical and religious use was passed in 2022. A bill introduced in September 2026 would limit the personal-use exemption to people over 25.
TT.note: Amounts are in Trinidad and Tobago dollars. The September 2026 age bill had not passed when this guide was written.

adult-use.short: Decriminalised in private; no legal market
adult-use.detail: The Dangerous Drugs (Amendment) Act 2019 made small amounts and four plants lawful to hold, with no age limit written in. Smoking or using cannabis in a public place is an offence with a fine of up to $50,000; police must issue a fixed penalty notice for it, and private dwellings not used commercially are outside the definition of a public place. A Bill introduced on September 30, 2026 would restrict the exemption to people over 25 and give under-25s a fixed penalty or rehabilitative programme instead.
adult-use.citation: Dangerous Drugs (Amendment) Act 2019, ss. 3, 5(2), 5A, 5B; Bill Essentials (Oct 2 2026)

medical.short: Licensing law passed in 2022
medical.detail: The Cannabis Control Act (Act No. 10 of 2022, assented June 17, 2022) sets up the Trinidad and Tobago Cannabis Licensing Authority to control cannabis for medicinal, therapeutic, scientific and religious purposes. Parliament's own record of the Act does not show a proclamation date, so this guide does not say how far patient access has started.
medical.citation: Parliament progress record for Act No. 10 of 2022

possession.short: Up to 30 grams is not an offence
possession.detail: Possessing up to 30 grams of cannabis or 5 grams of resin is not an offence. From 30 to 60 grams (5 to 10 grams of resin) the court fine is $50,000, but police issue a fixed penalty notice of $2,000 payable within 14 days that ends liability. From 60 to 100 grams (10 to 14 grams of resin) the fine is $75,000. Unpaid fines can be replaced with community service.
possession.citation: Dangerous Drugs (Amendment) Act 2019, ss. 5(2)(f), 5(2A)-(2D), 5B

home-grow.short: Up to four plants
home-grow.detail: A person does not commit an offence by cultivating or possessing up to four growing cannabis plants, and that is excluded from the trafficking offence. The Act does not say whether the limit is per person or per household.
home-grow.citation: Dangerous Drugs (Amendment) Act 2019, ss. 5(2)(g), 5(3A)

driving.short: Up to $250,000 and five years
driving.detail: Operating or being in actual physical control of a motor vehicle, aircraft or ship under the influence of cannabis carries a fine of $250,000 and up to five years in prison. The 2026 Bill would raise the fine to $500,000.
driving.citation: Dangerous Drugs (Amendment) Act 2019, s. 5C; Bill Essentials (Oct 2 2026)

record-relief.short: Small-possession records expunged
record-relief.detail: The Commissioner of Police must expunge records from before the 2019 Act for possession of up to 100 grams of cannabis or 14 grams of resin, and anyone convicted of that may apply to have the conviction expunged and then seek a pardon. People charged before the Act with up to 60 grams could apply to the court for a discharge.
record-relief.citation: Dangerous Drugs (Amendment) Act 2019, s. 5D

experiment.text: Cannabis on a school bus or where children gather for school, sport or culture carries the same $250,000 and five-year penalty as driving high, whatever the amount.

differences.title: What is different about Trinidad and Tobago
points: Small amounts and four plants are simply not an offence, with tickets for the next tier up.
Record clean-up reaches back to 100 grams, well above the new personal-use amount.
A 2026 bill proposes an age line of 25 for the personal-use exemption.

BB.name: Barbados
BB.summary: Cannabis is still illegal for adult use. Since a 2021 amendment, police can hand someone with 14 grams or less a $200 fixed penalty ticket instead of charging them, and older convictions for that amount are treated as expunged. Medical cannabis is legal on a doctor's prescription, filled by a pharmacist; the first licensed dispensary opened in 2025. Rastafari can use cannabis as a sacrament only in permitted places of worship.
BB.note: Amounts are in Barbados dollars. The Acts are cited from the bill texts on Parliament's site.

adult-use.short: Illegal; small amounts get a ticket
adult-use.detail: Recreational use is not permitted, the licensing authority said in 2025. Possession remains an offence; the 2021 fixed-penalty system only changes how small amounts are handled. In July 2026 the High Court upheld the drug law against a constitutional challenge, noting that home use and home growing outside the sacramental scheme remain regulated by it.
adult-use.citation: Barbados Today (Jun 14 2025; Jun 1 2024; Jul 31 2026)

medical.short: Doctor's prescription, filled by a pharmacist
medical.detail: Under the Medicinal Cannabis Industry Act 2019, medicinal cannabis may be used only when a medical practitioner prescribes or recommends it. A pharmacist dispenses it at a pharmacy or licensed therapeutic facility on a prescription and valid ID, with no more than a 30-day supply at a time for ongoing use. Under-21s need a practitioner's certificate and parental consent. The Act covers non-resident visitors holding a prescription or written recommendation, with the dispensing procedure left to regulations. The first licensed dispensary, Island Therapeutics in Worthing, opened in June 2025.
medical.citation: Medicinal Cannabis Industry Act 2019, ss. 2, 25-29, 42; Barbados Today (Jun 14 2025)

buying.detail: There is no recreational sale. Medicinal cannabis is not sold to walk-in customers, and selling or giving it away at conventions, trade shows or events is prohibited. Using cannabis that is not prescribed carries up to $100,000 or 10 years under the medical Act.
buying.citation: Barbados Today (Jun 14 2025); Medicinal Cannabis Industry Act 2019, ss. 25(3), 40

possession.short: Up to 14 grams: a $200 ticket
possession.detail: If police believe someone had 14 grams or less, they can serve a fixed penalty notice instead of a charge. Paying $200 within 30 days ends liability to conviction. People under 18 must also attend the National Council on Substance Abuse for assessment within 14 days; adults can be referred if they seem addicted. Not paying is an offence with a $1,000 fine, and someone who disputes the possession can be prosecuted instead.
possession.citation: Drug Abuse (Prevention and Control) (Amendment) Act 2021, s. 6A; Barbados Today (Jun 1 2024)

home-grow.short: Not allowed outside the sacramental scheme
home-grow.detail: Cultivation is licensed for the medical industry, and the sacramental scheme allows growing only on the premises of a permitted place of worship. The High Court noted in July 2026 that private home cultivation remains regulated under the general drug law.
home-grow.citation: Medicinal Cannabis Industry Act 2019, ss. 30-31; Sacramental Cannabis Act 2019 draft; Barbados Today (Jul 31 2026)

record-relief.short: Small-possession convictions deemed expunged
record-relief.detail: A person convicted of possessing 14 grams or less is deemed rehabilitated once the sentence is served, and the conviction is deemed expunged, despite the general rehabilitation-of-offenders law.
record-relief.citation: Drug Abuse (Prevention and Control) (Amendment) Act 2021, s. 6B

experiment.text: Rastafari places of worship can hold a sacramental use permit to grow and use cannabis on the premises, not within 600 metres of a school, and get a one-day permit to carry up to 14 grams to a worship event in a public place. Nothing under the scheme may be sold.

differences.title: What is different about Barbados
points: Small possession is ticketed, but officials stress it is not decriminalised.
Medical cannabis goes through pharmacists, with a 30-day supply limit for ongoing use.
Sacramental use is tied to permitted places of worship, and the High Court has upheld that limit.

GD.name: Grenada
GD.summary: Since February 2026, possessing up to 56 grams of cannabis or 15 grams of resin is not an offence, and up to four plants per household are allowed. Under-21s found with a personal amount are referred to counselling instead of being charged. Smoking near public places is a ticketable offence and near schools a serious one. Old convictions for these amounts are expunged. There is no legal market yet; the government must bring in a separate law for a regulated industry.
GD.note: Amounts are in Eastern Caribbean dollars. The Cannabis Commission's FAQ page was defaced when checked, so the guide relies on the Act itself.

adult-use.short: Decriminalised; no legal sales yet
adult-use.detail: Act No. 1 of 2026, published on February 20, 2026, takes personal amounts and home plants out of the drug offences. Smoking or using cannabis within five metres of the entrance, exit, window or air intake of a public place, workplace or public transport is an offence: a $300 fixed penalty that is not a conviction, or up to $5,000 in court. Public places include beaches, parks, bars and government offices, but not private homes or registered Rastafari places of worship.
adult-use.citation: Drug Abuse (Prevention and Control) (Amendment) Act 2026, ss. 6(5), 13B, 13E, Ninth Schedule; Gazette (Feb 20 2026)

medical.short: Allowed on a practitioner's recommendation; industry law pending
medical.detail: Possession for medical or therapeutic use recommended by a medical or other licensed health practitioner is lawful, and importing a medicinal product is exempt when a doctor certifies a qualifying condition. The Act directs the Minister to develop separate legislation for a licensed medicinal, therapeutic, scientific and religious cannabis industry.
medical.citation: Drug Abuse (Prevention and Control) (Amendment) Act 2026, ss. 4(4), 6(6), 13D

buying.detail: The 2026 Act decriminalises possession and home growing but does not create a legal market. Licensing for a regulated industry is left to future legislation.
buying.citation: Drug Abuse (Prevention and Control) (Amendment) Act 2026, s. 13D; Caribbean National Weekly (Jan 21 2026)

possession.short: Up to 56 grams is not an offence
possession.detail: Possessing up to 56 grams of cannabis or 15 grams of resin is not an offence. A child under 18 found with that amount is referred to the Child Protection Authority, and a young person aged 18 to 20 to a drug counselling programme; neither can be arrested or charged and no record results, though the cannabis can be forfeited. 71 grams of cannabis or 30 grams of resin is a trafficable quantity.
possession.citation: Drug Abuse (Prevention and Control) (Amendment) Act 2026, ss. 6(5), 6A, Second and Eighth Schedules

home-grow.short: Up to four plants per household
home-grow.detail: The cultivation and possession offences do not apply to four or fewer cannabis plants on any premises, and where a building houses more than one household, each household counts separately. The Act does not require registration for this. Rastafari adherents aged 21 or over can be authorised by Gazette order to grow on designated land for sacramental use.
home-grow.citation: Drug Abuse (Prevention and Control) (Amendment) Act 2026, ss. 11(3)-(4), 13A

record-relief.short: Old small-amount convictions expunged
record-relief.detail: Convictions before the Act for possessing or using up to 56 grams or 15 grams of resin, growing four or fewer plants, or having pipes or equipment are treated as spent and expunged. People can apply to the Rehabilitation of Offenders Board, which can also act on its own, and pending proceedings for such conduct must be discontinued.
record-relief.citation: Drug Abuse (Prevention and Control) (Amendment) Act 2026, Schedule (new s. 19A, Rehabilitation of Offenders Act)

experiment.text: Smoking or using cannabis on school premises, or in a public place within 100 yards of a school during school hours, can bring a fine of up to $250,000 or seven years in prison, and more on indictment.

differences.title: What is different about Grenada
points: Young adults aged 18 to 20 are sent to counselling rather than charged for a personal amount.
Smoking rules are measured in metres from doorways and windows, not just "in public".
Expungement covers past convictions for home plants and pipes, not only possession.

BS.name: Bahamas
BS.summary: Recreational cannabis is illegal. The Cannabis Act passed in 2024 sets a $250 fine instead of a criminal charge for up to 30 grams and legalises medical and Rastafari religious use, but it has been brought in slowly: arrests for small amounts were still reported in 2025, and the medical licensing portal had not opened as of July 2026.
BS.note: The Cannabis Act text and its commencement orders were not opened; this guide relies on the Prime Minister's speech and Nassau news reports.

adult-use.short: Recreational use stays illegal
adult-use.detail: The Prime Minister told Parliament in July 2024 that recreational use is not permitted under the reform package, and that possession of small amounts would still be unlawful, with a $250 fine replacing a criminal conviction. Smoking cannabis in public places is an offence.
adult-use.citation: OPM, Prime Minister's debate contribution (Jul 15 2024)

medical.short: Legal in law; licensing not yet open
medical.detail: The 2024 package legalises medical cannabis for listed conditions such as chronic pain, epilepsy and glaucoma. Prescribers must be trained, dispensaries must have a licensed pharmacist, and foreign medical cannabis cards from listed jurisdictions are to be recognised. As of July 22, 2026, the Cannabis Authority's online licensing portal, including a personal medical use category, had not opened.
medical.citation: OPM (Jul 15 2024); The Tribune (Jul 22 2026)

buying.detail: There is no recreational sale. Medical sales are to go through licensed dispensaries, including pharmacies with a separate licence and a physically separate dispensary area, but licensing had not started as of July 2026. Cultivation, sale and transport licences are reserved for wholly Bahamian-owned businesses.
buying.citation: The Tribune (Jul 22 2026); OPM (Jul 15 2024)

possession.short: $250 fine on paper; prosecutions still reported
possession.detail: The Cannabis Act 2024 sets a $250 fine instead of criminal penalties for possession of up to 30 grams. In February 2025 only the provisions creating the Cannabis Authority were in force, and in September 2025 the Authority's chairman said people caught with small amounts were still being prosecuted, which he had raised with officials several times.
possession.citation: The Tribune (Feb 5 2025; Sep 24 2025)

record-relief.short: Apply to have old 30-gram convictions expunged
record-relief.detail: People convicted in the past of possessing 30 grams or less can apply to the Minister to have the record expunged, the Prime Minister said in presenting the bills.
record-relief.citation: OPM (Jul 15 2024)

experiment.text: Rastafari religious use has its own licences: a licensed group's leader may give cannabis only to members at a place of worship, and an unaffiliated believer can be licensed to use it in a secured private space at home.

differences.title: What is different about the Bahamas
points: The law has been passed but brought into effect in stages, so practice can lag behind the text.
Foreign medical cannabis cards from listed jurisdictions are meant to be recognised.
Most industry licences are reserved for Bahamian owners.

LC.name: Saint Lucia
LC.summary: Since September 2021, possessing 30 grams or less of cannabis or resin is not an offence, and a person may grow up to four plants at their home. Smoking in public is still an offence with a fine of up to $1,500 that does not go on a criminal record. There is no legal market yet; a draft Cannabis and Industrial Hemp Bill went to public consultation in 2025.
LC.note: Amounts are in Eastern Caribbean dollars.

adult-use.short: Decriminalised in private; no legal market
adult-use.detail: The 2021 amendment made personal amounts lawful to hold. Smoking any part of the cannabis plant in a public place, including bars, restaurants, clubs and government offices, is an offence with a fine of up to $1,500 that does not form part of a criminal record, and owners who knowingly allow it also commit an offence. A privately occupied home not used commercially is not a public place. A child or young person found with cannabis must attend an approved drug counselling programme.
adult-use.citation: Drugs (Prevention of Misuse) (Amendment) Act 2021, ss. 5-6 (new ss. 14A, 27A)

buying.detail: There is no licensed market. A draft Cannabis and Industrial Hemp Bill covering farming, processing and sales of cannabis and hemp was released for public consultation, which closed on February 7, 2025; this guide did not find it enacted.
buying.citation: HempToday (Jan 2025)

possession.short: 30 grams or less is not an offence
possession.detail: A person who possesses 30 grams or less of cannabis or cannabis resin is not guilty of an offence, and prosecution and punishment under section 37 do not apply to that amount.
possession.citation: Drugs (Prevention of Misuse) Act, s. 8A (inserted by Act 13 of 2021)

home-grow.short: Up to four plants at home
home-grow.detail: Under the Cannabis Cultivation Regulations of 2021, a person may grow no more than four cannabis plants at a time at his or her dwelling-house, and the regulation also limits the total where more than one person lives there. Growing may be indoors, in one room, or outdoors, and the regulations restrict growing near school premises.
home-grow.citation: Drugs (Prevention of Misuse) (Cannabis Cultivation) Regulations, SI 208/2021, regs. 4-8

experiment.text: A ticket for smoking in public stays off your criminal record, but owners and managers of bars, restaurants and clubs can be fined too if they knowingly let people smoke there.

differences.title: What is different about Saint Lucia
points: Possession, home growing and the public-smoking rule all came in one 2021 amendment.
Home growing has its own regulations, down to growing indoors in a single room.
A wider cannabis and hemp industry law was still at the draft stage in 2025.

DM.name: Dominica
DM.summary: Since an October 2020 amendment to the Drugs (Prevention of Misuse) Act, adults 18 and over are not guilty of an offence for having 28 grams or less of cannabis; more than that is still unlawful. There is no legal market, and a medical cannabis framework was still being developed in 2025.
DM.note: The 2020 amendment text was not reachable; this guide relies on news reports of the debate and a 2025 government release.

adult-use.short: Small amounts decriminalised; no legal market
adult-use.detail: Parliament amended the Drugs (Prevention of Misuse) Act on October 26, 2020, decriminalising small quantities for personal and religious use, the National Security Minister said. He added that cannabis should not be decriminalised entirely without restrictions.
adult-use.citation: Jamaica Observer (Oct 26 2020); CARICOM Today (Oct 2020)

medical.short: No medical framework yet
medical.detail: The government held a National Cannabis Symposium on July 9-10, 2025, and its 2024/2025 budget provides for developing legislation on safe access to medicinal cannabis. A regulated medical industry had not been set up as of that release.
medical.citation: Government Information Service (Jul 11 2025)

possession.short: Up to 28 grams for adults
possession.detail: People aged 18 and over who have 28 grams or less are not guilty of an offence under section 72 of the Act. Having more than 28 grams remains unlawful.
possession.citation: Drugs (Prevention of Misuse) (Amendment) Act 2020, as reported by CARICOM Today and the Jamaica Observer

record-relief.short: Government said 28-gram records would be cleared
record-relief.detail: Presenting the amendment, the minister said the government was taking steps to expunge the records of people in respect of possession of 28 grams. How this works in practice was not found.
record-relief.citation: Jamaica Observer (Oct 26 2020); CARICOM Today (Oct 2020)

experiment.text: In 2020 the Prime Minister said a medical cannabis industry would be hard to run alone, with Dominica sitting between the French territories of Martinique and Guadeloupe.

differences.title: What is different about Dominica
points: The 28-gram line applies only to adults aged 18 and over.
Government work in 2025 centred on a framework for a regulated medical cannabis industry.

BM.name: Bermuda
BM.summary: Since December 20, 2017, simple possession of 7 grams or less of cannabis is not a criminal offence, but cannabis is still a controlled drug: police can seize any amount, and smoking, growing, selling and importing remain illegal. Bermuda's 2022 bill for a licensed cannabis market was blocked when the UK instructed the Governor not to give assent.
BM.note: Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory, so the UK has a say over laws that touch its treaty obligations.

adult-use.short: Decriminalised possession only; use is illegal
adult-use.detail: The 2017 amendment does not legalise cannabis. Smoking it in public or private places, growing, trafficking and importing all remain illegal, and the government has reminded the public that decriminalisation is not legalisation.
adult-use.citation: Government of Bermuda fact sheet (2017); Ministerial Statement

buying.detail: There is no licensed market. The Cannabis Licensing Bill 2022 would have created one, but on September 6, 2022 the Governor announced she had been instructed not to assent to it, because the UK judged it inconsistent with the 1961 and 1971 UN drug conventions.
buying.citation: Governor's statement (gov.uk, Sep 6 2022)

possession.short: 7 grams or less is not a criminal offence
possession.detail: Criminal offences no longer apply to simple possession of 7 grams or less by any person. Police may still seize any amount, weigh and test it, and search a home, vessel or vehicle if they suspect another offence such as intent to supply. More than 7 grams can lead to arrest, prosecution and a conviction.
possession.citation: Government of Bermuda fact sheet on the 2017 Amendment Act, items 3 and 6-9

home-grow.short: Growing is illegal
home-grow.detail: The 2017 Act does not make it legal to cultivate cannabis in any quantity.
home-grow.citation: Government of Bermuda fact sheet (2017), item 3

record-relief.short: Old convictions are not erased
record-relief.detail: The 2017 Act does not erase cannabis convictions from before it took effect, and the government notes it cannot guarantee anyone will not be stopped when travelling to the United States.
record-relief.citation: Government of Bermuda fact sheet (2017), items 4-5

experiment.text: The UK said in 2022 that Bermuda can still legislate for medicinal, scientific and some industrial cannabis, and can decriminalise small personal amounts, but not legalise sales in shops or cafés.

differences.title: What is different about Bermuda
points: Possession of a small amount is not a crime, but using cannabis anywhere still is.
A 2022 bill for a licensed market was stopped by the UK.
Past convictions stay on record, which can matter at the US border.

KY.name: Cayman Islands
KY.summary: Cannabis is illegal except for prescribed medical extracts and tinctures. Possession and use still carry prison terms on the books. Voters backed decriminalising small amounts in an April 2025 referendum, and the Law Reform Commission was taking public submissions on how to do it until September 1, 2026.
KY.note: Amounts are in Cayman Islands dollars. Reform was under consultation when this guide was written.

adult-use.short: Illegal; reform under consultation
adult-use.detail: Consuming cannabis carries a fine of up to $3,000 and up to three years in prison under the Misuse of Drugs Act, rising to $10,000 and ten years for a third conviction. On April 30, 2025, 55.64% of voters in a non-binding referendum supported decriminalising consumption and possession of small amounts. Cabinet referred the question to the Law Reform Commission on June 27, 2025, and its discussion paper took submissions until September 1, 2026.
adult-use.citation: Law Reform Commission discussion paper (Jul 1 2026), citing the Misuse of Drugs Act (2026 Revision)

medical.short: Prescribed extracts and tinctures only
medical.detail: Section 2A of the Misuse of Drugs Act permits cannabis extracts and tinctures for medical or therapeutic use on a prescription from a medical doctor.
medical.citation: Misuse of Drugs Act s. 2A, as cited in the Law Reform Commission paper (Jul 1 2026)

possession.short: Still a crime
possession.detail: Possessing less than one pound of cannabis or resin carries a fine of up to $20,000 and up to seven years in prison under the current Act, with up to ten years for a repeat conviction. The 2025 referendum result has not yet changed the law.
possession.citation: Law Reform Commission discussion paper (Jul 1 2026)

record-relief.short: Parliament asked for an expungement law
record-relief.detail: On October 9, 2024 Parliament passed a motion asking the Government to consider amending the spent convictions law so that convictions for possessing one ounce or less for personal use can be expunged. The motion does not itself expunge records.
record-relief.citation: Parliament of the Cayman Islands, PMM No. 2 of 2024-2025

experiment.text: The Law Reform Commission's paper compares decriminalisation models from elsewhere, including some that allow personal cultivation, but it had not settled on a Cayman model when consultation opened.

differences.title: What is different about the Cayman Islands
points: Voters have already backed decriminalisation, but the law has not changed yet.
Medical access is limited to prescribed extracts and tinctures.
On paper, possession of under a pound can still mean years in prison.

travel_warnings.detail: Possession of even very small quantities can lead to the death penalty, according to UK travel advice. Singapore classes cannabis as a Class A drug, with up to 10 years in prison and a fine of up to S$20,000 for consumption. Drug use detected on arrival can mean arrest.
Zero tolerance. Possessing, using, making or trafficking drugs can bring long prison sentences or the death penalty. Airports scan transit passengers' bags for cannabis.

Possession, trafficking and manufacture of any illegal drug, including cannabis, are serious offences. British travellers have been caught carrying cannabis while only transiting. Australia lists Malaysia among countries that apply the death penalty to drug offences.

Possession is a crime outside a COFEPRIS permit, and visitors have no permit. The U.S. government warns that drug possession and use, including medical marijuana, is illegal in Mexico and may result in a lengthy jail sentence.
UAE authorities treat drugs found in your bloodstream as possession, so use before arrival can lead to charges. Some CBD products are illegal.
Since December 12, 2024, using cannabis is a crime. Possession, use and transfer each carry up to 7 years in prison, and import carries 1 to 10 years.
Possession or use can bring up to 5 years in prison, and smuggling carries much longer terms, followed by deportation and an entry ban (Thai embassy warning).

travel_warnings.risk: Up to 10 years at the border
travel_warnings.detail: Since June 2026, bringing cannabis across Thailand's border can mean up to 10 years in prison, a fine of up to 500,000 baht, or both.
Australia's government lists these among countries that apply the death penalty to drug offences.

texas_concentrates.text: In Texas, THC concentrates (vape oil, wax, most edibles) are not treated as marijuana. They are Penalty Group 2 controlled substances, and possessing less than 1 gram is a state jail felony: 180 days to 2 years and a fine of up to $10,000.
texas_concentrates.citation: Tex. Health & Safety Code 481.103 and 481.116; NORML penalty table
